story.intro: We redesigned a 20 cc syringe for Indian healthcare practitioners, focusing on how they hold, operate and read it. I developed the selected concept; Varun Panda and I shared the research and 3D-printed prototype work over four weeks. My teammate created the Maya model.

blocks.text: Our 20 cc syringe concept changes the thumb rest, finger flange, barrel grip and scale markings. The aim is to give smaller hands a more secure hold while keeping the dose visible. My teammate modelled it in Maya, and we 3D printed a prototype to explore its shape and contact with the hand.

blocks.text: Six changes to the contact surfaces

items.title: Concave thumb rest
items.body: I curved the thumb rest inward to support the thumb pad when pushing the plunger.

items.title: Butterfly finger flange
items.body: Four rounded lobes give the fingers contact surfaces at different angles around the barrel.

items.title: Transparent, ridged grip
items.body: Ridges aim to help fingers hold the barrel while its transparent material keeps the fluid visible.

items.title: Major rings, minor arcs
items.body: Thick lines run around the barrel for major values. Thin, short curved marks keep the smaller readings from crowding the scale.

items.title: Curved underside support
items.body: Curves beneath the flanges support more of the thumb when drawing fluid, with the aim of spreading pressure over a wider area.

items.title: Supported flange joints
items.body: Reports of flange failure led me to add curved material where the flange joins the barrel. Its load capacity still needs testing.

blocks.text: What the pilot ratings showed

blocks.before: Physical effort stayed at 4.0/10. Plunger smoothness fell from 6.3 to 5.3 and perceived dosage accuracy from 6.7 to 5.0.
blocks.after: Grip and thumb-strain impressions improved. Across all 21 attributes, 14 rated higher, two were unchanged and five rated lower.
blocks.note: These are subjective impressions. The overall mean rose from 4.14 to 5.62/10, but it cannot outweigh a weaker result on control or dosing. The full results appear in Evaluation.

blocks.text: Source: our HFID course report, p.14, Table 10. These are pilot questionnaire ratings, not measured clinical performance.

We returned to the same hospital, where nurses tried the physical prototype and answered questions about how it felt in use. This Kansei Engineering questionnaire captures impressions of comfort and control; functional performance still needs task-based testing.

Indian healthcare practitioners with smaller hands can struggle to reach the plunger and keep a secure hold on a 20 cc syringe. Repeated thumb pressure, awkward wrist positions and slipping with gloves or wet hands were the problems we set out to address.

items.title: 74 mm working stroke
items.body: The plunger travels 74 mm—92.5% of the 80 mm maximum thumb-to-index-finger span reported for a smaller Indian female hand (5th percentile). This leaves little spare reach.

items.title: 30–56 N reported injection force
items.body: Published studies report this range for thick liquids, alongside an average thumb-to-fingertip pinch strength of 35.2 N for Indian adult women. We did not measure injection force.

items.title: 32 QEC wrist/hand score
items.body: Our exploratory Quick Exposure Check (QEC), a posture-risk screening method, rated wrist and hand exposure as high. Practitioner feedback also described thumb-pad pressure, slipping and awkward wrist positions.

blocks.text: Source: our HFID course report, p.7 for QEC and practitioner feedback; pp.8–10 for the literature and hand-measurement review. Literature force values were not measured on our prototype.
The design question
How might we improve grip and thumb support for smaller Indian hands while keeping the syringe familiar to use?

We combined published studies, a practitioner questionnaire, an exploratory posture-risk assessment and hand measurements. We measured existing syringes with a digital calliper, then grouped practitioner feedback into an affinity map to decide which parts of the design needed attention.
Who contributed the evidence

blocks.caption: Separate research records and unresolved sample information
rows: The paper describes routine syringe users and includes nurse, physician and laboratory-technician roles.
Pages 4 and 7 use 23 in prose but 25 in a profile table and chart caption. The response sheet must resolve that conflict; no single sample total is asserted here.
A single assessment team recorded wrist/hand exposure of 32, alongside shoulder/arm and back scores.
Number of observed practitioners and agreement between independent assessors are not established. This is an exploratory exposure screen.
The approved case records nurses handling the physical print and rating both devices across 21 terms.
Pilot rater count is unconfirmed. The paper describes existing-first order, but the exact execution and counterbalancing record remain incomplete.

blocks.text: Method source: HFID paper pp.4, 6–7 and 20; physical-print account: approved interactive case, 19 October 2026. Questionnaire respondents and pilot raters are separate sample questions. Rounded ratings are not evidence of a particular pilot size.

blocks.text: Holding and pushing needed different responses

Grip problems and pushing-force problems formed separate groups. Changing the parts that touch the hand could improve support and grip; reducing plunger force would also require work on the mechanism.

items.title: Thumb pressure → support the thumb pad
items.body: Literature and feedback described pressure over a small contact area. We explored inward-curved rests with rounded edges.

items.title: Slipping → give fingers a secure hold
items.body: Feedback about gloves and wet hands led us towards barrel ridges and curved flange surfaces.

items.title: Posture and reading → keep the dose visible
items.body: Reading the scale could require turning the barrel or changing grip. Thick major rings and short minor marks aimed to preserve a clearer hierarchy.

items.title: Hand and device dimensions → check reach and clearance
items.body: Plunger travel, contact width and ridge gaps need different hand measurements. We checked smaller-hand reach separately from space for larger fingers.

blocks.text: I explored the thumb rest, flange, barrel grip and scale as individual points of contact. Varun explored the syringe as a whole. We reviewed both approaches and selected my component-level concept for Maya modelling and 3D printing.

items.title: Push

items.title: Hold

items.title: Draw fluid

items.title: Wider palm support
items.body: A broad wing would support the palm as well as the fingers.

items.title: Colour-coded markings

blocks.text: The selected direction

My component-level concept moved forward. Its grip, thumb support, flange shape, joint supports and scale were carried into the Maya model and printed prototype. Varun’s sketches remained an alternative; we continued the research and development together.

That selection narrowed what we built to the contact surfaces and scale. It did not introduce a new force-reducing mechanism or shorten the 74 mm stroke, so the original concerns about effort and reach remained open.
A current review of the trade-off

blocks.before: A whole-form wing could bring the palm into the support area, but it also changes the overall hold and would need its own dimensional and handling checks.
blocks.after: The component route keeps the familiar barrel and makes thumb, finger and scale details easier to inspect separately. It also leaves the original stroke and actuation mechanism unchanged.
blocks.note: Retrospective design review · November 2026. This explains the scope I would assess now; it is not a recovered historical selection test. My concept remains the selected direction, with shared research and development credited to Varun and me.

blocks.text: I developed the selected concept around three decisions: distinguish major and minor scale marks, support the thumb when pushing and drawing fluid, and strengthen the flange connections. The dimensional review below also identifies parts that still need resizing.

visual.alt: Final concept sketch showing the syringe in side view and the four-lobed butterfly flange in top view.
visual.caption: Final concept · Side and top views

items.title: Wrap the major lines
items.body: Thick rings keep major values visible around the barrel. Thin, short curved brackets prevent the smaller readings from filling the surface with lines.

items.title: Support the thumb in both directions
items.body: The concave plunger rest supports pushing; underside flange curves support the thumb while drawing fluid.

items.title: Support the flange connection
items.body: Curved material at the joints was included in the model. Its load capacity still needs testing.

blocks.before: If every scale mark wrapped around the barrel, the additional lines could make small readings harder to identify.
blocks.after: Use two levels of emphasis: thick full rings for major values and thin, short arcs for minor readings.
blocks.note: The design aims to keep detail readable. Scale-reading accuracy remains a separate testing question.

blocks.text: The proposed values are the paper’s design hypotheses, not dimensions validated by this print. The thumb-rest question is especially useful: a smaller concave rest received a better strain rating, but that does not tell us its contact pressure. I would test the actual contact and hand fit before treating any target as settled.
What still needs revision

The flange contact width and gap between grip ridges are both 16 mm; the revised requirement is at least 22 mm. The plunger stroke remains 74 mm. Thumb pressure should be measured before choosing a new thumb-rest diameter.

Designing for smaller hands does not mean making every part smaller. Reach has to work for smaller hands, while contact surfaces and gaps also need room for larger fingers. The 16 mm widths did not meet that revised requirement; the new shape alone did not resolve hand fit.
We still need to measure thumb pressure and joint load. The current contact changes should not be treated as proof of reduced plunger effort.

My teammate built the selected concept in Autodesk Maya. We then worked on the 3D-printed prototype together. The model brought the barrel, scale and redesigned contact surfaces together; the print let us examine size, grip position and contact with the hand.

blocks.text: Holding the print made its size and contact points tangible. We then returned to the hospital for the pilot evaluation.

The approved case confirms that nurses handled the physical print. The retained records do not establish whether it had a working fluid path. I therefore separate holding and appearance impressions from any claim about moving fluid or delivering a dose.

The pilot gave mixed results. Nurses rated the grip more favourably, but physical effort stayed at 4.0/10. Plunger smoothness fell from 6.3 to 5.3, and perceived dosage accuracy fell from 6.7 to 5.0. These findings made control and dosing priorities for the next version.

Nurses tried the physical prototype at the same hospital, then rated how it felt using a Kansei Engineering questionnaire. We compared the existing syringe and prototype across 21 attributes on a 1–10 scale. Higher means a more favourable impression, including less slipping or strain for those terms.

The pilot rater count is unconfirmed. The paper describes rating the existing syringe first and prototype second; its limitations qualify that account, and execution/counterbalancing records are incomplete. We cannot infer a sample size from the rounded means.

Because a working fluid path is not established, the smoothness, control and dosage ratings may reflect handling or expectation rather than an executed dosing task. They still identify questions to investigate; they do not measure delivered-dose error.
Effort and dosing remain open

items.title: Physical effort · 4.0 → 4.0
items.body: The contact shape changed, but the physical-effort rating stayed the same. Any claim of lower effort would need a force measurement and, potentially, a change to the mechanism.

items.title: Plunger smoothness · 6.3 → 5.3
items.body: The lower rating makes plunger movement a testing priority. A more secure grip does not by itself establish smooth movement.

items.title: Dosage accuracy · 6.7 → 5.0
items.body: Test dose setting from different viewing angles and measure the fluid delivered. The rating identifies a concern; it does not quantify a dosing error.

blocks.text: Grip impressions improved

visual.alt: Pilot ratings on a common zero-to-ten scale: grip slipperiness 2.3 to 7.0, thumb strain 2.0 to 6.7 and glove usability 2.0 to 6.0; physical effort 4.0 to 4.0, plunger smoothness 6.3 to 5.3 and dosage accuracy 6.7 to 5.0.
visual.caption: Selected pilot ratings · Existing syringe and prototype on the same 0–10 scale

blocks.text: Grip slipperiness and thumb strain ratings each rose by 4.7 points; glove usability rose by 4.0. These were areas we aimed to improve, but we did not test each design feature separately.
Read the overall mean alongside those trade-offs

items.body: Mean across all 21 attributes: a rise of 1.48 rating points. The project paper reports this as a 35.7% higher mean relative to the original. It is a change in subjective ratings, not a measured physical benefit.

items.title: 14 higher · 2 unchanged · 5 lower
items.body: The overall mean does not show every trade-off. Grip and comfort improved in the ratings, while effort and dosing remained open.

items.title: Subjective pilot evaluation
items.body: These ratings describe nurses’ impressions. They do not measure injection force, thumb pressure, wrist angles or the amount of fluid delivered.

blocks.text: Separate perception from performance

Measurement readability rose from 4.0 to 6.0, while dosage accuracy fell from 6.7 to 5.0. The ratings describe different things: being able to read the markings and feeling able to set a dose accurately. That disagreement is a reason to test the complete dosing task, rather than treating the clearer-looking scale as a finished improvement.
Fit across the full hand-size range remains unconfirmed. A follow-up study should measure task performance and vary which syringe each participant tries first to check for an order effect.

The pilot gave us more favourable grip ratings, but effort stayed the same and dosage accuracy rated lower. I would revise hand fit and test dose setting, pressure and force before taking the concept further.

items.title: Break down the interface. Keep the task in view.
items.body: Major rings and short minor marks aim to reduce scale clutter. Their value still depends on whether users can read and set a dose accurately.

items.title: Evaluate comfort, control and effort separately.
items.body: Grip ratings improved, effort stayed the same and dosage accuracy rated lower. Each result needs attention; the overall mean cannot replace them.

items.title: Check who each dimension fits.
items.body: We initially used female 95th-percentile measurements for finger space. A later check against larger male fingers showed that the 16 mm contact width and ridge gaps were too small. I would check smaller and larger hands before finalising dimensions.

blocks.text: What I would test next

items.title: Dose setting · mL and percentage error
items.body: Compare a working prototype with the existing syringe using a reference scale. Test readings from several angles and weigh the delivered fluid.

items.title: Pressure and effort · kPa and newtons
items.body: Use pressure-sensitive film for thumb pressure and a force gauge for plunger effort. Use those results to revise the thumb rest and any mechanism intended to reduce effort.

items.title: Hand fit, posture and slip
items.body: Include practitioners with smaller and larger hands, record their measurements and vary the testing order. Revisit contact widths, ridge spacing and plunger travel alongside repeat ratings.

blocks.text: I would resolve the contact dimensions before that next round, then prioritise dose setting and plunger movement because their pilot ratings fell. Repeat comfort ratings alongside the task measurements so a better overall impression cannot hide a weaker result on a critical part of use.
Presenting the work at Meraki

visual.alt: Lakshya beside his syringe redesign display at Meraki.
visual.caption: Presenting the syringe redesign at Meraki. Photo from my project presentation.

blocks.text: We presented the research and 3D-printed prototype at Meraki. Jurors appreciated the depth of the work and our explanation of the design.

The redesign was also shortlisted after the first review round for research-paper presentation at HWWE 2026. The December 2026 event is still ahead at the time of this case update, and publication remains subject to jury review.

outcome.title: Current outcome
outcome.text: We built and piloted a physical form. Effort ratings were unchanged; smoothness and perceived dosage accuracy fell, while grip ratings improved. The mean across 21 attributes rose from 4.14 to 5.62/10. Pilot size and counterbalancing remain unconfirmed; a working fluid path and measured performance are not established.
